title: Why we should get rid of learning styles and start again.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton, who admits he long liked learning styles, argues the field should be set aside until it can be rebuilt on firmer ground. He gives five reasons: there is no agreement on what learning styles are (VAK, Kolb, Fleming, Felder and others all compete), no agreement on what they look like, no reliable way of identifying who has which style, no clarity on what they are for in the learning process, and a weak research base. He notes teachers often assign styles with good intentions but little evidence. Drawing on his own principle that evidence is the most important factor affecting learning, he concludes the current support is not there. He is careful to say children do differ and teachers should respond to this, but the label of learning style is a poor way to do it.
points: The case against learning styles rests less on a single refutation than on definitional chaos: competing models by Vester, Kolb, Fleming, Felder and others.
Even if styles existed, Skelton can only see them mattering at the attention or noticing stage of learning, and finds no evidence they do.
Research tends to measure student preferences rather than actual learning gains, and isolating the variable is difficult.
Labelling pupils with inconsistent categories may hardwire false beliefs about how they can learn, and planning for styles wastes teacher time.
He keeps the broader belief that learners differ and that teachers should respond, but suspends the learning styles framework until evidence supports it.
quotes: Learning styles are the marmite of learning. You either like them or you loathe them. (I have always sort of liked them. Until now.)

My problem is that I have come to see that the general debate about learning styles is completely unhelpful to anyone who wants to know whether learning styles are truly a facto that positively affects learning. Here’s six reasons why this has happened.
Unsurprisingly, if we can’t agree first what learning styles are and second what they look like, it is going to be very difficult to be able to say for sure which children have which learning styles.

Given what we know about how learning happens, if learning styles are a factor that affects learning it can only be at the very first stage of attention or noticing. In other words, it could be that learning styles might be about how that first stimulus gets noticed and gains access to the cell body or an existing neuronal constellation.

I have always been aware that, like playing Mozart to babies, recommended learning style approaches were ahead of any evidence that might support them. As someone who puts Evidence as the most important factor that affects learning, I have to face up to the fact that, currently, the evidence about the helpfulness of learning styles just isn’t there.

I have changed my mind about the certainty with which I previously thought of learning styles. It’s now time to step back for a while until we can be clearer about what they are, about how we can tell who has them, about where they are best used in the learning process and about the quality of the research and evidence base that indicates that they do make a difference to learning and whether those differences relate to knowledge, skills or understanding.
But we really need to be sure that the time and energy learning styles use up for teachers, children, students and others is worth it. I’m not sure it is right now.
